before.lead: Bringing an appliance for assessment is different from approving a repair or choosing a replacement. I help Washington County businesses make that sequence clear while showing which service routes are currently offered.
before.decisionTitle: Explain the diagnostic decision and its different next steps before the appliance arrives.
before.decision:
B&R Discount Appliances in Beaverton currently describes in-shop repairs and temporarily unavailable mobile service. Its published diagnostic terms distinguish the credit applied when a repair is approved from the smaller store credit offered when the customer upgrades instead. Declining repair has a separate collection or recycling outcome.

For a repair-and-retail website, I would draw the assessment sequence before designing the first inquiry. Explain how the item reaches the shop, what the initial diagnostic charge covers and which decision the customer makes after receiving an estimate. The approved repair, replacement purchase and declined-work routes need their own wording; a general phrase such as credit toward service should not blur them together.

The owner supplies current terms, accepted appliance categories and the staff process for estimates and approval. I would test a customer who chooses replacement after assessment and another who asks for a home visit while that service is unavailable. The website should explain the right next step without promising a full repair credit on a replacement or implying that a delivery offer is an in-home repair appointment. Public inquiry examples should use known model details and observed symptoms, not repair instructions or payment credentials.

before.lead: A free membership entry does not mean the products in a recurring allocation are free. I help Yamhill County businesses explain what happens after signup and what customers must do before an order is collected or shipped.
before.decisionTitle: Explain club signup, allocation and collection as separate stages.
before.decision:
Yamhill Valley Vineyards' Estate Wine Club page displays a no-fee membership item and says the team follows up to complete signup. It separately describes recurring wine allocations and explains that uncollected will-call selections are shipped after the stated holding period. Its policy also asks members to update delivery information ahead of shipment.

For a membership-based producer, I would show the stages before presenting a single join button: the signup request, staff completion of membership, the next allocation and its collection or delivery arrangement. A zero price beside the membership item should be explained alongside the actual product commitment. The business supplies and approves that explanation; the website should not infer billing behavior from an item label alone.

The wider project can connect the offer page with the existing member instructions. Test a member who cannot collect an allocation during the holding period: they need to understand the approved next step and how to discuss an address or delivery change. The site should preserve the relevant allocation and request without claiming that a message has already changed an account or shipment. Keep account, billing and age-verification steps in the established secure service, with a clear staff contact for unresolved questions.

scopes.supplies: Current offer, recurring allocation description, signup confirmation and the terms the business has approved.
scopes.check: A zero-priced membership item is not described as a free wine allocation or proof that signup is complete.

pages: Advance information changes and staff contact
scopes.request: Identify the allocation and ask about the required collection or delivery change through the established member route.
scopes.supplies: Current pickup and shipping instructions, update deadlines, member-service destination and the wording that confirms an accepted change.
scopes.check: An address-change question is not treated as an account update or a guarantee that an already planned shipment will change.
